name: Qualia
statement: The redness of red, the sting of pain, the taste of coffee: the raw felt qualities of experience.
statementAccent: the raw felt qualities of experience
meaning: Qualia, singular quale, are the subjective, qualitative properties of conscious experience, the felt, phenomenal qualities of what it is like to have a particular experience. Examples include the redness of seeing red, the painfulness of pain, the taste of coffee, and the smell of a rose: the specific qualitative feel of each experience, as opposed to its functional role or physical description. The term comes from the Latin qualis, meaning of what kind or quality, and it was introduced into philosophy in its modern sense by C. I. Lewis in 1929. Qualia are often characterized by a set of features, spelled out critically by Daniel Dennett, as ineffable, meaning they cannot be fully described in words; intrinsic, meaning non-relational; private, meaning not straightforwardly comparable between people; and directly or immediately apprehensible in consciousness. Qualia are central to arguments against physicalism, the view that everything is physical, since they seem to resist physical or functional explanation. These arguments include the knowledge argument, or Mary's room, the inverted-spectrum thought experiment, the explanatory gap, and philosophical zombies. Qualia are a central and contested concept in the philosophy of mind and the study of consciousness, and some philosophers deny that qualia, as traditionally conceived, exist at all.
mechanism: Qualia are what make conscious experiences feel the particular way they do. When a person sees a ripe tomato, undergoes a headache, or tastes something bitter, there is not only information processing and behavioral disposition but also a subjective character to the experience, a way it feels from the inside; qualia are these felt qualitative characters. Philosophers use qualia to draw a distinction between the objective, third-person description of a mental state, in terms of neural activity or functional role, and its subjective, first-person feel, and they argue that the two can come apart. This is the basis of the classic anti-physicalist arguments. In the knowledge argument, a scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision but has never seen color seems to learn something new, the quale of red, when she first sees it, suggesting there are facts about experience that are not physical facts. In the inverted-spectrum scenario, two people might be functionally identical yet have systematically different color qualia, one seeing as red what the other sees as green, suggesting qualia are not fixed by function. Philosophical zombies, physical duplicates of us that lack any qualia, are invoked to suggest that experience is something over and above the physical. Each argument turns on the apparent gap between the physical or functional facts and the qualia, the felt qualities that seem to escape them.

examples.text: The particular felt quality of seeing red, as opposed to the wavelength of light or the neural activity, is a quale.
A scientist who knew all the physical facts about color yet learned something new on first seeing red suggests qualia are non-physical.
Qualia are often said to be ineffable, intrinsic, private, and directly apprehensible, features Daniel Dennett critically examined.

variants.name: Dennett's denial
variants.text: Daniel Dennett's argument that nothing has all the properties traditionally ascribed to qualia, so there are no qualia at all.

whyItMatters: Qualia are a central and pivotal concept in the philosophy of mind, because they name the aspect of consciousness, its subjective felt quality, that seems hardest to fit into a physical account of the world. By focusing attention on what it is like to have an experience, the concept of qualia sharpens the deepest questions about consciousness and provides the fuel for the most important arguments against physicalism, including the knowledge argument, the inverted spectrum, the explanatory gap, and philosophical zombies, all of which press the claim that the felt qualities of experience cannot be captured by physical or functional descriptions. These arguments and the concept behind them structure the debate between physicalists, dualists, and their rivals, and they connect directly to the hard problem of consciousness. Qualia also raise puzzles about privacy and knowledge of other minds, since one person cannot directly access another's felt experience. The concept is contested, and the very question of whether qualia, as traditionally conceived, exist is itself a major debate that has shaped the field.

distinguish the quale from the objective description, and note that the two seem able to come apart.
use cases like Mary's room, inverted spectra, and zombies to argue that qualia escape physical explanation.

limits: Qualia are a contested concept, and their very existence, as traditionally understood, is disputed. Daniel Dennett, in his essay Quining Qualia, argued that nothing has all the properties commonly ascribed to qualia, being at once ineffable, intrinsic, private, and directly apprehensible, and concluded that there are no qualia in that strong sense. Functionalists and representationalists analyze the qualitative character of experience differently, in terms of function or representational content, rather than as intrinsic non-physical properties. The anti-physicalist arguments built on qualia are themselves widely contested, and it is telling that Frank Jackson, who devised the knowledge argument, later abandoned it and became a physicalist.
misreadings: Qualia are not simply the objective properties of the stimulus or the brain; they are the subjective felt qualities of experience, which is precisely why they are said to resist physical description. Their existence as traditionally conceived is not settled, since Dennett argues nothing fits the bill and functionalists analyze experience differently. And the arguments built on qualia are not decisive against physicalism, since even the knowledge argument's author recanted, so treating qualia as obvious physical facts, as uncontroversially real, or as decisively refuting physicalism, misreads a central but deeply contested concept.
origin: The subjective, qualitative properties of conscious experience, named in their modern sense by C. I. Lewis in 1929; central to arguments against physicalism and to the philosophy of consciousness, though their existence is disputed.
